summary: Build a Sieve of Eratosthenes up to R once, so "is x prime?" becomes a list lookup (T11). Then count the numbers in [L, R] that are prime and read the same backwards (T2).

blocks.title: Read L and R from one line
blocks.text: Both numbers are typed on ONE line, so `split()` + `map(int, …)`. Two `input()` calls would hang.

blocks.title: Start with everything marked prime
blocks.text: `is_prime[x]` will say whether x is prime. The list has R + 1 slots so that index R itself exists.

blocks.title: 0 and 1 are not prime
blocks.text: 1 is NOT prime — a classic hidden test with L = 1. The `if R >= 1` guard avoids an `IndexError` if the list only has one slot.

blocks.title: Cross out multiples
blocks.text: For each prime `i`, all its multiples are not prime. We only need `i` up to √R, because any composite number ≤ R has a factor that small. We start at `i * i` since smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes.

blocks.title: Count prime palindromes in the range
blocks.text: `range(L, R + 1)` includes R. `str(x) == str(x)[::-1]` checks the palindrome by comparing the text with its reverse. The prime check is just a lookup now.

complexity: Sieve time O(R log log R); with R ≤ 100,000 that is a few hundred thousand steps (~0.05 s).
pitfalls: Trial-dividing every number in the range — much slower.
